a: Along with the other half of Manasseh, the Reubenites and the Gadites had already received their inheritance.
p: The Hebrew begins this verse "With it," with nothing clear for "it" to refer to. The Greek has a longer text here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: with it the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance
readings.plain: Along with the other half of Manasseh, the Reubenites and the Gadites had already received their inheritance.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.en: ... and the half-tribe of Manasseh. From the Jordan to the Great Sea westward you shall give it; the Great Sea will be the border. To the two tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh, to Reuben and Gad, Moses gave ...
readings.plain: To the two tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh, to Reuben and to Gad, Moses had already given their inheritance.

why: The half-tribe named at the end of 13:7 is the western half, which received no land east of the Jordan, so the Hebrew "with it" does not fit. Most commentators think a scribe's eye skipped from one mention of the half-tribe of Manasseh to the next and dropped a line that the Greek still has. The NRSV and NAB note the problem. The Plain English follows the Hebrew but supplies "the other half of Manasseh" to make sense of "with it."
b: The Greek also adds to the end of 13:7: "From the Jordan to the Great Sea westward you shall give it; the Great Sea will be the border."

a: Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.
t: A great man or a mother city?
p: The Hebrew calls Arba the greatest man of the Anakim. The Greek calls Hebron their chief city.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: the great man among the Anakim
readings.plain: Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.en: this was the mother city of the Anakim
readings.plain: It was the chief city of the Anakim.

why: The Hebrew agrees with 15:13 and 21:11, which call Arba the father of Anak. The Greek seems to have read the Hebrew ha'adam ("the man") as a form of em ("mother"), giving "mother city." The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

a: she pressed him to ask her father for a field.
p: In the Hebrew, Achsah urges Othniel to ask for a field. In the Greek of Joshua she tells him she will ask herself. In the Latin, Othniel urges her.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); also Judges 1:14 in Hebrew
readings.en: and she urged him to ask her father for a field
readings.plain: she pressed him to ask her father for a field.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.orig: καὶ συνεβουλεύσατο αὐτῷ λέγουσα Αἰτήσομαι τὸν πατέρα μου ἀγρόν
readings.en: and she advised him, saying, 'I will ask my father for a field'
readings.plain: she advised him, saying, "I will ask my father for a field."

readings.w: Latin Vulgate; compare the Greek of Judges 1:14, "he urged her"
readings.orig: suasa est a viro suo ut peteret a patre suo agrum
readings.en: she was persuaded by her husband to ask her father for a field
readings.plain: she was urged by her husband to ask her father for a field.

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading: she urges him, yet in 15:19 she makes the request herself. The Greek of Joshua removes the tension by having her announce that she will ask. The Latin of Joshua, like the Greek of Judges 1:14 ("he urged her"), turns the roles around so that Othniel urges her. Both look like attempts to smooth the story. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew, as most translations do.

a: Biziothiah
p: A town named Biziothiah, or a slightly different word, "its villages"? The Greek and Nehemiah 11:27 suggest the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Biziothiah

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts); compare Nehemiah 11:27, "Beersheba and its villages"
readings.plain: with its villages

why: The two Hebrew words look alike (bizyotyah and uvenoteha, "and its daughters"). Many scholars think the Greek reading is original, and some modern versions follow it. No town Biziothiah is known elsewhere. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew name but notes that "Beersheba with its villages" is quite possibly right.

a: Dumah
p: The Leningrad Codex reads Rumah. Other Hebrew manuscripts and printed Bibles read Dumah.

readings.w: Other Hebrew manuscripts and the printed Rabbinic Bible (followed by the KJV and most translations)
readings.plain: Dumah

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Rumah

why: Hebrew d (ד) and r (ר) look almost the same and are often confused. A village called Khirbet Domeh, southwest of Hebron, keeps the name Dumah in the right area. So the Plain English reads Dumah.

a: six towns, with their villages.
p: The Greek adds a whole district of eleven towns here, including Tekoa and Bethlehem. It is missing from the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.plain: six towns, with their villages.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.orig: ... Θεκω καὶ Εφραθα, αὕτη ἐστὶν Βαιθλεεμ ... πόλεις ἕνδεκα καὶ αἱ κῶμαι αὐτῶν
readings.en: ... Tekoa and Ephratha, that is Bethlehem ... eleven cities and their villages
readings.plain: six towns, with their villages. Tekoa, Ephrathah (that is, Bethlehem), Peor, Etam, Kulon, Tatam, Sores, Karem, Gallim, Bether and Manocho: eleven towns, with their villages.

why: Most scholars think the Greek keeps a district that dropped out of the Hebrew. A copyist's eye could easily jump from one "towns, with their villages" to the next, skipping the lines between. Without it, Judah's list has no Bethlehem, no Tekoa, and a gap in the hills south of Jerusalem, where most of these names can be found: Tekoa, Bethlehem, Etam, Bether (Battir), Karem (Ein Karem). Some translations, such as the RSV and NRSV, put the district in the text. The Plain English follows the Hebrew but gives the Greek here, since it is very likely original.
b: The spelling of several names differs between Greek manuscripts. This district matters to Christian readers because Bethlehem, David's town and the birthplace of Jesus (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:1), is otherwise missing from Judah's list.

a: to this day, but they have been put to forced labor.
p: The Greek replaces the forced-labor clause with the story of a pharaoh burning Gezer and giving it to his daughter, as told in 1 Kings 9:16.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: until this day, and they became forced laborers
readings.plain: to this day, but they have been put to forced labor.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: to this day, until Pharaoh king of Egypt came up, captured the town and burned it with fire. He killed the Canaanites, the Perizzites and those living in Gezer, and Pharaoh gave it to his daughter as a dowry.

why: The Greek line is drawn from 1 Kings 9:16, which tells how a pharaoh captured Gezer and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife. It looks like a later scribe's explanation of how Gezer finally came under Israel's control. The Greek has no forced-labor clause. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.
b: The wording of the Greek addition differs slightly among manuscripts.

a: The border went out westward
p: The Hebrew says the border went "westward," which is hard to fit on the map. The NRSV corrects it to "to Ephron."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the border went out westward
readings.plain: The border went out westward

readings.w: Conjecture adopted by the NRSV, based on 15:9
readings.en: and the border went out to Ephron
readings.plain: The border went out to Ephron

why: No manuscript reads "to Ephron." It is a scholar's guess based on 15:9, where the same line passes "the towns of Mount Ephron." The Plain English keeps the Hebrew; see the note on this verse.

a: to the slope facing the Arabah
p: The Hebrew says the border passed the slope facing the Arabah. The Greek names the town of Beth-arabah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: to the shoulder opposite the Arabah
readings.plain: to the slope facing the Arabah

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: to the slope of Beth-arabah

why: Beth-arabah lies on this line: it marks Judah's north border (15:6) and is one of Benjamin's towns (18:22). For that reason many translations, among them the NIV, ESV and BSB, follow the Greek. The Hebrew "facing" and "Beth" differ by only a few letters. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew, which still makes sense.

a: Ebron
p: Some Hebrew manuscripts read Abdon, the name of the Levite town of Asher in 21:30.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Ebron

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; compare 21:30 and 1 Chronicles 6:74
readings.plain: Abdon

why: Again d and r are confused. Abdon (Khirbet Abdeh, inland from Achzib) is a known town of Asher; Ebron is not otherwise known. Many scholars prefer Abdon. The Plain English keeps the Leningrad Codex's reading and gives the alternative here.

a: But the territory of the Danites slipped out of their hands.
p: The Greek expands 19:47–48 with lines like Judges 1:34–35: the Amorites pressed Dan into the hills.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and the territory of the Danites went out from them
readings.plain: But the territory of the Danites slipped out of their hands.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: But the Danites did not drive out the Amorites, who pressed them into the hill country and would not let them come down into the valley. They took from the Danites the border of their share.

why: The Greek lines are close to Judges 1:34–35, and the Greek also reorders the end of 19:47–48. Many scholars think a translator or scribe filled out the terse Hebrew "went out from them" from Judges; a few think the Greek keeps older text. Either way, both explain why Dan moved north. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

a: When he has fled to one of these cities, he must stand at the entrance to the city gate and tell the elders of that city what happened. The elders will then bring him inside to join them, and they will give him a place to live with them.
t: A shorter law in the Greek (1)
p: The Greek lacks 20:4–5 and the second half of 20:6. These three entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: and he shall flee to one of these cities ...
readings.plain: When he has fled to one of these cities, he must stand at the entrance to the city gate and tell the elders of that city what happened. The elders will then bring him inside to join them, and they will give him a place to live with them.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)

why: Many scholars, such as Alexander Rofé and Emanuel Tov, think the shorter Greek reflects an earlier Hebrew text, and that the Hebrew was later filled out with the wording of Deuteronomy 19 (elders, "had not hated him in the past"). Others think the Greek translator shortened a repetitive passage. The Plain English follows the full Hebrew text, which every Hebrew manuscript has.

a: Should the avenger of blood come after him, they are not to give the killer up into his hand. He struck down his neighbor without meaning to, and he had not hated him in the past.
t: A shorter law in the Greek (2)
p: This verse, with 20:4 and the end of 20:6, is missing from the Greek. The entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: and if the avenger of blood pursues him ...
readings.plain: Should the avenger of blood come after him, they are not to give the killer up into his hand. He struck down his neighbor without meaning to, and he had not hated him in the past.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)

why: See 20:4. The phrase "had not hated him in the past" is Deuteronomy's (Deuteronomy 19:4, 6), which supports the view that this verse was added from Deuteronomy to an older, shorter law.

a: , and until the high priest of that time has died. Then the killer may go back to the town he fled from and to his own house there
t: A shorter law in the Greek (3)
p: The Greek ends the verse at the trial, without the high priest's death. Goes with 20:4–5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: until the death of the high priest ...
readings.plain: , and until the high priest of that time has died. Then the killer may go back to the town he fled from and to his own house there

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)

why: The high priest's death comes from Numbers 35:25–28. If the shorter Greek is older, the Hebrew later added it to complete the law. The Plain English follows the Hebrew. See 20:4.

a: From the tribe of Reuben: Bezer with its pastureland, Jahaz with its pastureland,
t: Reuben's towns: missing in some manuscripts (1)
p: 21:36–37 are missing from the Leningrad Codex and some other Hebrew manuscripts. These two entries go together.

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles; Septuagint; Targum; Vulgate; compare 1 Chronicles 6:78–79
readings.en: and from the tribe of Reuben, Bezer and its pasturelands ...
readings.plain: From the tribe of Reuben: Bezer with its pastureland, Jahaz with its pastureland,

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) and some other medieval Hebrew manuscripts

why: Without these verses the Merarites get only eight towns, not the twelve of 21:7 and 21:40, and Reuben, which 21:7 names, gives nothing. The verses are almost certainly original and were dropped by a copyist, perhaps because 21:35 and 21:37 both end "four towns." The source text used for this site prints them from other manuscripts. 1 Chronicles 6:78–79 lists the same four towns.
b: Medieval Jewish scholars already noticed that some careful manuscripts lacked these verses; the printed Rabbinic Bibles, and so the KJV, included them.

a: Kedemoth with its pastureland and Mephaath with its pastureland: four towns.
t: Reuben's towns: missing in some manuscripts (2)
p: Goes with 21:36: both verses are missing from the Leningrad Codex.

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles; Septuagint; Targum; Vulgate; compare 1 Chronicles 6:79
readings.plain: Kedemoth with its pastureland and Mephaath with its pastureland: four towns.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) and some other medieval Hebrew manuscripts

why: See 21:36. The counts in 21:7 and 21:40 need these four towns.

a: So it was with all these towns.
p: The Greek adds a passage here: Joshua's own town again, and the flint knives used at Gilgal, laid up there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: So it was with all these towns.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: So it was with all these towns. Joshua finished dividing the land by its borders, and at the LORD's command the Israelites gave Joshua a share. They gave him the town he asked for, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He built up the town and lived in it. And Joshua took the flint knives with which he had circumcised the Israelites who were born on the way in the wilderness, and he put them in Timnath-serah.

why: The first part repeats 19:49–50. The knives come from 5:2–9, where Joshua circumcised the new generation with flint knives. The Greek mentions them again at Joshua's burial (see 24:30). Most scholars see these as additions in the Greek tradition, though a few think the Hebrew lost them. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

a: gave the altar its name
p: The Hebrew says they named the altar but does not give the name. Some manuscripts add "Ed," "Witness."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: they called the altar: for it is a witness
readings.plain: gave the altar its name

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Syriac Peshitta; KJV ("called the altar Ed", with Ed in italics as a supplied word)
readings.plain: named the altar Witness

why: The Hebrew may mean that the explanation itself is the name, or a word may have dropped out. Since the next words say "it is a witness" (ed), the name was almost certainly Ed, "Witness." The Plain English keeps the Hebrew wording, which already gives the meaning.

a: at Shechem
p: The Greek sets the covenant at Shiloh, where the tent was, not Shechem. Goes with 24:25.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.plain: at Shechem

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: at Shiloh

why: Shechem is surely original: it fits the burial of Joseph there (24:32), the oak and the old covenant site (Genesis 35:4; Deuteronomy 27), and the "sanctuary of the LORD" at Shechem (24:26). A Greek scribe probably changed it to Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood (18:1), perhaps because a covenant "before God" seemed to belong at the sanctuary, or to keep holiness away from Shechem, which by then was the Samaritans' center.

a: the two kings of the Amorites
p: The Hebrew says two kings (Sihon and Og). The Greek says twelve.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: the two kings of the Amorite
readings.plain: the two kings of the Amorites

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: the twelve kings of the Amorites

why: "The two kings of the Amorites" is a fixed phrase for Sihon and Og (2:10; 9:10), whose defeat was the standard example of God's help. But they ruled east of the Jordan, and this verse comes after the crossing, which may be why the Greek has "twelve": perhaps a way to make the list fit the kings west of the Jordan (compare the list in chapter 12). The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

a: at Shechem
p: Again the Greek says Shiloh. Goes with 24:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.plain: at Shechem

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: at Shiloh

a: north of Mount Gaash.
p: The Greek adds that the flint knives of Gilgal were buried with Joshua.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: north of Mount Gaash.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: north of Mount Gaash. There they put with him in the tomb where they buried him the flint knives with which he had circumcised the Israelites at Gilgal, when he brought them out of Egypt, as the LORD had ordered them. And they are there to this day.

why: This goes with the Greek addition at 21:42. It ties Joshua's grave to the circumcision at Gilgal (5:2–9). Most scholars see it as part of a longer Greek edition of Joshua's ending. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

a: which had been given to him in the hill country of Ephraim.
p: The Greek continues the story: the ark carried among the people, Phinehas as priest, and Israel's first slide into idolatry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: which was given to him in the hill country of Ephraim
readings.plain: which had been given to him in the hill country of Ephraim.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD, and other manuscripts)
readings.plain: which had been given to him in the hill country of Ephraim. On that day the Israelites took the ark of God and carried it around among them. Phinehas served as priest in place of his father Eleazar until he died, and he was buried at his own Gibeah. Then the Israelites went away, each to his own place and his own town. And the Israelites worshiped Astarte and Ashtaroth and the gods of the nations around them, and the LORD handed them over to Eglon king of Moab, and he ruled them eighteen years.

why: The Greek ending runs on into the story of Judges (Judges 2:11–13; 3:12–14), linking the two books without a break. Most scholars think it is a later bridge, though some think an older Hebrew text had it. Every Hebrew manuscript ends at Eleazar's burial. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek ending shows that Joshua and Judges were read as one continuing story. In the Hebrew canon they are the first two of the Former Prophets, with Samuel and Kings.
